quote: An arrangement is a simple lottery if— (a) persons are required to pay in order to participate in the arrangement, (b) in the course of the arrangement one or more prizes are allocated to one or more members of a class, and (c) the prizes are allocated by a process which relies wholly on chance.
finding: Three cumulative limbs: payment + prizes + allocation wholly by chance. Paid-entry prize draws stay outside 'lottery' only by removing the payment limb (Sch 2 para 8 free route) or the chance limb (genuine skill, s.14(5)). Frames every platform RAFFLE EDGE studies.

quote: (c) the prizes are allocated by a series of processes, and (d) the first of those processes relies wholly on chance.
finding: Multi-stage mechanics (e.g. random shortlist then a 'skill' tiebreak, or instant-win then main draw) are still a lottery if the FIRST stage is pure chance and payment is required.

source_name: Gambling Act 2005 - s.14(5)(a) skill treated as chance
quote: A process which requires persons to exercise skill or judgment or to display knowledge shall be treated for the purposes of this section as relying wholly on chance if— (a) the requirement cannot reasonably be expected to prevent a significant proportion of persons who participate
finding: A trivial skill question does not convert a paid draw into a prize competition. 'Significant proportion' is undefined in the Act.

source_name: Gambling Act 2005 - s.14(5)(b) skill test second limb
quote: receiving a prize, and (b) the requirement cannot reasonably be expected to prevent a significant proportion of persons who wish to participate in that arrangement from doing so.
finding: Limbs (a) and (b) are joined by 'and': skill is treated as chance only if it neither stops a significant proportion winning NOR deters a significant proportion entering. For player strategy: on skill-only sites there is no statutory free route.

quote: The Secretary of State may by regulations provide that an arrangement of a specified kind is to be or not to be treated as a lottery for the purposes of this Act;
finding: The free-draw/skill boundary can be moved by secondary legislation without a new Act. Business models dependent on free postal entry carry regulatory-change risk.

source_name: Gambling Act 2005 - Sch 2 para 2(c) meaning of payment
quote: (c) paying for goods or services at a price or rate which reflects the opportunity to participate in an arrangement.
finding: 'Payment' is broad: buying a product priced to include entry counts. A 'free' route bundled with any priced purchase is not free.

source_name: Gambling Act 2005 - Sch 2 para 5(2)(b) ordinary post
quote: (b) ordinary post means ordinary first-class or second-class post (without special arrangements for delivery).
finding: Postal free entries must be acceptable by ordinary 1st/2nd class post; an operator demanding recorded/special delivery would fail the condition. The cost of a stamp is NOT 'payment' (para 5(1)).

source_name: Gambling Act 2005 - Sch 2 para 8(1)(a)-(b) free-entry choice
quote: each individual who is eligible to participate has a choice whether to participate by paying or by sending a communication, (b) the communication mentioned in paragraph (a) may be— (i) a letter sent by ordinary post, or (ii) another method of communication which is neither
finding: Core free-draw exemption. Postal route is expressly sufficient by itself; a non-postal route must be 'neither more expensive nor less convenient than entering the lottery by paying'. Player strategy: free postal entries are a statutory entitlement, not a concession.

source_name: Gambling Act 2005 - Sch 2 para 8(1)(c)-(d) publicity and equal treatment
quote: (c) the choice is publicised in such a way as to be likely to come to the attention of each individual who proposes to participate, and (d) the system for allocating prizes does not differentiate between those who participate by paying and those who participate by sending a communication.
finding: Free entries must have exactly equal chances in the allocation system. This is the legal hook for a draw-verification product (testing that postal entries are entered and weighted equally) and for player strategy EV maths (a free entry = one paid ticket).

source_name: Gambling Act 2005 - Sch 2 para 7 payment to claim
quote: a requirement to pay in order to take possession of a prize which has or may have been allocated to a person under an arrangement shall be treated as a requirement to pay in order to participate in the arrangement.
finding: Any fee to claim (delivery, admin, 'tax') turns a free draw into a payment-to-participate lottery. Useful red-flag field for a comparison site.

quote: Participating in a competition or other arrangement under which a person may win a prize is not gambling for the purposes of this Act unless it is— (a) gaming within the meaning of section 6, (b) participating in a lottery within the meaning of section 14,
finding: Genuine skill competitions are outside the Act entirely; they need no free route. Whether a 'skill question' is genuine is decided via s.14(5).

source_name: Gambling Act 2005 - s.258(1) offence: promoting a lottery
quote: A person commits an offence if he promotes a lottery unless— (a) the exception in subsection (2) or (3) applies, or (b) the lottery is an exempt lottery.
finding: An operator whose free route fails Sch 2 para 8 is promoting an unlicensed lottery. Relevant to anyone who also 'promotes' it (see s.252).

quote: It is a defence for a person charged with an offence under this section to show that he reasonably believed that— (a) he was not committing the offence by reason of subsection (1)(b), (2) or (3), (b) that the arrangement to which the charge relates was not a lottery,
finding: A documented due-diligence check of each listed operator's free route may support a reasonable-belief position for a comparison/affiliate site. Hypothesis only.

quote: (c) arranges for the distribution or publication of promotional material, (d) possesses promotional material with a view to its distribution or publication, (e) makes other arrangements to advertise a lottery, (f) invites a person to participate in a lottery,
finding: KEY RISK for the comparison/affiliate model: publishing promotional material for, or inviting people to enter, a draw that is in law an illegal lottery may itself be 'promoting' it. Affiliate links with commission increase exposure.

quote: Promoters must specify the number and nature of prizes or gifts, if applicable.
finding: Data field for comparison: number and nature of prizes must be published by operators.

source_name: CAP Code (UK Code of Non-broadcast Advertising), Section 08 Promotional marketing - rule 8.20
quote: Promoters must not exaggerate consumers' chances of winning prizes.
finding: A 'value' or 'best odds' site must avoid the same fault in its own claims (see DMCCA Sch 20 para 18).

source_name: CAP Code (UK Code of Non-broadcast Advertising), Section 08 Promotional marketing - rule 8.24
quote: Promoters of prize draws must ensure that prizes are awarded in accordance with the laws of chance and, unless winners are selected by a computer process that produces verifiably random results, by an independent person, or under the supervision of an independent person.
finding: Draw-verification demand: same structure as DCMS 2.2. 'Verifiably random' is undefined.

source_name: CAP Code (UK Code of Non-broadcast Advertising), Section 08 Promotional marketing - rule 8.25 instant wins
quote: verification must take the form of an independently audited statement that all prizes have been distributed, or made available for distribution, in that manner.
finding: Instant-win promotions need an independently audited statement. A concrete, CAP-anchored product for a verification business.

source_name: CAP Code (UK Code of Non-broadcast Advertising), Section 08 Promotional marketing - rule 8.28.5 winner information
quote: Promoters must either publish or make available information that indicates that a valid award took place – ordinarily the surname and county of major prizewinners and, if applicable, their winning entries.
finding: Explains why winner names appear publicly. Publication is for proof of award, not for third-party reuse. Entrants may object.

source_name: CAP Code (UK Code of Non-broadcast Advertising), Section 08 Promotional marketing - rule 8.28.5 privacy
quote: The privacy of prizewinners must not be prejudiced by the publication of personal information
finding: Supports the project rule of not collecting winner names.

source_name: CAP Code (UK Code of Non-broadcast Advertising), Section 08 Promotional marketing - rule 8.17.4.e closing dates
quote: Closing dates must not be changed unless unavoidable circumstances beyond the control of the promoter make it necessary
finding: Draw-date extensions are measurable. A comparison site could flag them (factually, with evidence).

source_name: ASA AdviceOnline - Promotional marketing: High value prize promotions (17 Jun 2026) - cash alternatives
quote: It is unlikely to be considered acceptable to award a cash prize of a significantly lower value than the advertised prize.
finding: Prize-value claims: compare advertised value with the cash alternative. Advice is non-binding.

source_name: ASA AdviceOnline - High value prize promotions - conditional prizes
quote: sometimes the prize advertised is only awarded if the promotion reaches a certain number of paid entries.
finding: The ASA recognises sales-threshold prizes as a problem pattern. This is a data field for comparison and value scoring.

source_name: ASA AdviceOnline - Promotional marketing: Free entry routes (17 Jun 2026) - presentation
quote: The free entry route should be presented clearly, and it will not be sufficient to only reference this in small print at the bottom of a page, or in full terms and conditions.
finding: Objective test usable in a free-route prominence audit.

source_name: ASA AdviceOnline - Free entry routes - online free entry
quote: Directing participants to a website address where they can enter for free is likely to be considered a free entry route.
finding: Online free-entry forms are accepted in principle; the cost and convenience test still applies.

source_name: ASA AdviceOnline - Free entry routes - status of advice
quote: It does not constitute legal advice. It does not bind CAP, CAP advisory panels or the Advertising Standards Authority.
finding: AdviceOnline is persuasive, not binding. The Code rules themselves bind marketers.

source_name: CAP Code, Section 03 Misleading advertising - rule 3.1
quote: Marketing communications must not materially mislead or be likely to do so.
finding: Applies to a comparison/value site's own marketing (e.g. 'best value draws').

source_name: CAP Code, Section 03 Misleading advertising - rule 3.7 substantiation
quote: marketers must hold documentary evidence to prove claims that consumers are likely to regard as objective and that are capable of objective substantiation.
finding: Any 'value', 'odds' or 'EV' claim needs an evidence file. The project's archived snapshots and A_CONFIRMED evidence model fit this requirement.

source_name: CAP Code, Section 03 Misleading advertising - rule 3.34 comparisons with identifiable competitors
quote: They must objectively compare one or more material, relevant, verifiable and representative feature of those products, which may include price.
finding: Applies where the comparison site markets its own product against competitors, and arguably to operator-versus-operator ranking pages. Rankings must use verifiable features.

source_name: CAP Code, Section 03 Misleading advertising - rule 3.38 price comparisons
quote: Marketing communications that include a price comparison must not mislead by failing to make the basis of the comparison clear.
finding: Methodology (ticket price, max tickets, prize value basis) must be stated clearly.

source_name: CAP Code, Section 03 Misleading advertising - rule 3.41 denigration
quote: must not discredit or denigrate another product, marketer, trade mark, trade name or other distinguishing mark.
finding: Negative findings about an operator (e.g. a weak free route) need careful, factual framing. Defamation risk is a separate issue.

source_name: Copyright and Rights in Databases Regulations 1997 (SI 1997/3032) - reg 13(1) database right
quote: A property right (“database right”) subsists, in accordance with this Part, in a database if there has been a substantial investment in obtaining, verifying or presenting the contents of the database.
finding: Operator draw-results and winner pages may attract database right if the investment was in obtaining, verifying or presenting the data. Investment in creating the draws themselves may not count (point for counsel).

source_name: Copyright and Rights in Databases Regulations 1997 (SI 1997/3032) - reg 16(1) infringement
quote: a person infringes database right in a database if, without the consent of the owner of the right, he extracts or re-utilises all or a substantial part of the contents of the database.
finding: Bulk collection of results feeds for a comparison site or dataset is the main risk.

source_name: Copyright and Rights in Databases Regulations 1997 (SI 1997/3032) - reg 16(2) repeated insubstantial parts
quote: the repeated and systematic extraction or re-utilisation of insubstantial parts of the contents of a database may amount to the extraction or re-utilisation of a substantial part of those contents.
finding: Scheduled polling of results pages, even a few fields at a time, can add up to infringement. This directly affects the 'collect' commands.

source_name: Copyright and Rights in Databases Regulations 1997 (SI 1997/3032) - reg 20(1) fair dealing exception
quote: (b) it is extracted for the purpose of illustration for teaching or research and not for any commercial purpose, and (c) the source is indicated.
finding: A narrow exception: non-commercial research, with the source cited, by a 'lawful user'. It covers the current research phase at best. It does not cover a comparison site, a paid verification service or a betting/strategy product.

source_name: ICO - What is the legitimate interests basis? (UK GDPR guidance) - lawful basis
quote: Legitimate interests is one of the seven lawful bases for handling personal information.
finding: Collecting winner names (surname and county) from public pages is processing personal data. Legitimate interests would be the likely basis and needs the three-part test.

source_name: ICO - What is the legitimate interests basis? (UK GDPR guidance) - necessity
quote: If you can achieve your purpose in a less intrusive way, the more intrusive way isn’t necessary.
finding: Win-rate and value analysis does not need names. Aggregate counts are a less intrusive route, so collecting names is unlikely to pass necessity. Supports the current no-names design.

source_name: ICO - What is the legitimate interests basis? (UK GDPR guidance) - reasonable expectations
quote: You must assess whether a person can reasonably expect what you intend to do.
finding: Winners consented to publication by the promoter (CAP 8.28.5), not to third-party profiling.

source_name: ICO - The lawful basis for web scraping to train generative AI models (consultation response) - web scraping risk
quote: Web scraping for generative AI training is a high-risk, invisible processing activity.
finding: The context is AI training, so this applies to RAFFLE EDGE by analogy only. It shows how the ICO views scraping personal data at scale.

source_name: Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations 2008 (SI 2008/1277) - reg 5 status
quote: revoked (6.4.2025 with transitional provisions and savings in relation to Pt. 4A, which is continued until regulations are made under s. 233 of the revoking Act) by Di
finding: The CPUTRs have been revoked. From 6 Apr 2025 the DMCCA 2024 Part 4 Chapter 1 regime applies.

source_name: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 - s.225(1)
quote: Unfair commercial practices are prohibited.
finding: Applies to operators and to the comparison site as a trader.

source_name: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 - s.225(3) 'commercial practice'
quote: “ commercial practice ” means an act or omission by a trader relating to the promotion or supply of— (a) the trader’s product to a consumer, (b) another trader’s product to a consumer,
finding: Promoting ANOTHER trader's product is covered, so a comparison or affiliate site is within scope for its rankings and value claims.

source_name: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 - s.226(1)(a)-(b) misleading actions
quote: (a) the provision of false or misleading information relating to a product, a trader or any other matter relevant to a transactional decision, (b) an overall presentation which is likely to deceive the average consumer
finding: Inflated prize values (operators), and misleading value scores or rankings (comparison site), are exposures.

source_name: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 - s.226(1)(d) code of conduct
quote: (d) a failure to comply with a requirement in a code of conduct to which subsection (5) applies in circumstances where the trader asserts that the trader acts in compliance with that code.
finding: An operator claiming DCMS Code compliance while breaching a firm Code requirement may be misleading. A verification site could test those claims.

source_name: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 - Sch 20 para 1
quote: Claiming to be a signatory to a code of conduct when the trader is not.
finding: Always banned. Signatory status changes often (55 removals on 19 Oct 2026), so a comparison site showing 'DCMS signatory' badges must re-check them against the dated list.

source_name: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 - Sch 20 para 18
quote: Claiming that products are able to facilitate winning in games of chance.
finding: HIGH RELEVANCE for any player-strategy or 'edge' product: marketing a tool or service as helping consumers win prize draws may fall within this always-banned practice. Pure statistical disclosure (EV per ticket) is arguably different.

source_name: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 - Sch 20 para 21
quote: Claiming to offer a competition or prize promotion without awarding the prizes described or a reasonable equivalent.
finding: Statutory counterpart of CAP 8.15.1. Non-award or under-value substitution is an always-banned practice for operators.

quote: he causes a computer to perform any function with intent to secure access to any program or data held in any computer
finding: Read with s.1(1)(b)-(c), the access must be unauthorised and known to be so. The fetcher's GET-only, no-login, robots-obeying, challenge-stops design keeps away from 'unauthorised' access. Breaching site terms alone is a contract issue, not clearly CMA.
